newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy tells Albania aid depends on fair elections.
newsitem.headline: Italy tells Albania aid depends on fair elections.

text.p: Italy said on Monday the international community would do its utmost to help with elections in Albania next month but that economic aid would depend on the vote being free and fair.
"Albania needs help," Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told a news conference after an international meeting in Rome on the crisis on Albania, where elections are scheduled for June 29.
"The international community is willing to provide the maximum help possible but the destiny of their country lies in their own hands," he said.

Dini said the main thing was that all sides took part in the election, seen as a crucial step in the restoration of normality. Preparations have been dogged by disputes between parties on how voting will be conducted and supervised.
Dini used his opening speech to the conference, attended by Albania's Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, to urge all parties to speed up reconciliation efforts.

"Without the consolidation of the national reconciliation process, without elections conducted in a safe and fair environment according to international standards, without rules of conduct shared and agreed by all parties in Albania, the conditions for recovery in the economic and financial fields will not be present," Dini said.
John Kornblum, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Canada and Europe, said the conference had provided "a tremendous concentration of effort" in the short time left before the vote.
The one-day meeting was attended by European mediator Franz Vranitzky, as well as senior officials from the European Union, the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
"The goal is elections which are conducted fairly, with a credible result," Kornblum told reporters.
"We certainly are determined to make them go off correctly and this conference has focused efforts in a way that gives every reason to hope that they will," he said.

Vranitzky, an envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said that although conditions for elections were not ideal, it would have been unworkable to restore public order before calling elections.
Albania slid towards anarchy in March when anger over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes boiled over into an uprising directed against President Sali Berisha.

Berisha installed an interim national unity government headed by Fino and agreed to early elections. But he refused a cabinet call at the weekend to lift a curfew imposed under a state of emergency decreed at the height of the troubles.

Although the situation has calmed since the arrival in April of an Italian-led multinational security force, large areas of the country remain outside government control and more than a million looted guns are in civilian hands.
Vranitzky said the security force, whose three-month United Nations mandate runs out on June 28, the day before the elections, would have to remain in Albania beyond polling day.
"It would be ridiculous to leave," he told a parliamentary hearing at Italy's Senate (upper house). He said he expected "a request for an extension and that an extension will be granted".
The 6,500-strong force has no mandate to disarm Albanians and there have been questions about whether it will be large enough to help oversee voting effectively.

Monday's meeting was to have paved the way for a ministerial conference on Albania in mid-June. Dini said the conference would now be held in July, after the Albanian elections and installation of a new government in Tirana.
